report.tagline: Europe's biggest independent app for buying train and coach tickets, used mostly in the UK, Spain, Italy and France.
report.simpleSummary: Trainline is an app for buying train tickets. In the UK there are many train companies and confusing fares, and Trainline shows all of them in one place with live times and platform updates. It has tricks like SplitSave, which breaks one journey into several cheaper tickets. Train companies pay Trainline a small commission, and customers often pay a small booking fee.

overview.whatItDoes: Trainline sells train and coach tickets from many operators in the UK and Europe in one app. It also gives live journey updates, delays and platform information. It has three parts: UK consumer, International consumer (Spain, Italy, France and more) and Trainline Solutions, which runs ticketing for train companies and business travel firms.
howItWorks: A traveller enters where and when they want to go, and Trainline shows trains and fares from all operators.
Trainline suggests cheaper options like SplitSave split tickets and Advance fares, and applies railcards.
The traveller pays in the app and gets an e-ticket or digital railcard on their phone.
On the day, the app shows live times, platform numbers, delays and refund help such as Delay Repay.
Train operators pay Trainline a commission, and customers pay a booking fee on many UK tickets.
overview.valueProposition: The simplest and often cheapest way to find and buy any train ticket, with live help on the day.

businessModel.summary: Trainline earns a small cut of each ticket it sells: commission from train operators and booking fees from customers. It earns about 7p for every £1 of tickets, plus fees from Trainline Solutions and ads.

revenueStreams.detail: Train companies pay a percentage of each ticket, set in the UK by industry rules.
Small fees per transaction, often under £2 in the UK.
Commissions and fees on Spanish, Italian and French tickets.
Fees from train operators and business travel firms using Trainline technology.
Ads, insurance and hotel partners in the app.

businessModel.pricing: Tickets cost the official fare. UK booking fees vary, typically under £2 per transaction. Not all fees are public.
costDrivers: Customer support for refunds and changes
businessModel.unitEconomics: Rough example. A customer buys a £60 London to Manchester ticket. Trainline might get about £3 in commission and £1 to £1.50 as a booking fee, so about £4 to £4.50, which matches its overall 7% take rate. Card fees cost maybe 50p, and support a few pence on average. In the UK, where most users come direct, it keeps most of that £4. In Spain and Italy it spends more on marketing to win each customer, which is why the International business only expects to break even in FY2027.

howTheyGetUsers: Free search results for routes and 'train times'
App store presence and word of mouth
Partnerships in Europe with operators like Trenitalia
whatBringsUsersBack: Habit of checking Trainline for any train trip
growth.moat: Trainline combines every UK operator, years of fare data for features like SplitSave and Price Prediction, and a well-known brand. Many people open it every week. A government app can sell the same tickets, but building better tools and the habit takes time.

competitors.name: Great British Railways (planned app)
competitors.positioning: Government-backed national rail body expected to run its own ticket app.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Trainline must win with better tools and savings, because GBR may have no fees and official status.

competitors.name: Train operator apps (LNER, Avanti, GWR)
competitors.positioning: Operators sell their own tickets with no booking fee.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Trainline covers all operators and offers split tickets across them.

competitors.name: Contactless and TfL
competitors.positioning: Tap in and out with a bank card, now on more routes around London.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Contactless removes the need for an app on short trips; Trainline is stronger on long trips.

competitors.name: Omio and Renfe or Trenitalia apps (Europe)
competitors.positioning: Multi-mode booking site and national operator apps.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Trainline is bigger in rail and offers deeper rail features.

pmLessons: Being an aggregator works when the market is confusing. Trainline wins because UK fares are complicated.
A government competitor changes the game. You must offer clear extra value, not just access.
Daily-use features like live times keep users coming back even when they are not buying.
Watch take rate as well as volume: Trainline's ticket sales grew faster than revenue.

interviewQuestions.question: Great British Railways launches a free app. How should Trainline respond?
interviewQuestions.hint: Name Trainline's unique value (SplitSave, multi-operator, Europe, live info), consider fee changes and subscriptions, and track retention.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you grow Trainline in Spain?
interviewQuestions.hint: Think about competing operators (Renfe, Iryo, Ouigo), tourists, pricing and marketing cost per customer. Define break-even metrics.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the north star for Trainline?
interviewQuestions.hint: Completed journeys, broken into active buyers, conversion, tickets per buyer and journey experience.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Trainline remove booking fees?
interviewQuestions.hint: Estimate fee revenue lost per booking against conversion and retention gains. Suggest testing on some routes.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure if SplitSave is worth it?
interviewQuestions.hint: Look at savings per user, conversion uplift, commission per ticket and repeat rate.
